claims.text: Formation and crystal-structure selection in noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles are governed by differential atomic diffusion rates and surface-energy disparities among the constituent metals during rapid thermal processing.
Slower heating with an isothermal hold near the onset of enhanced atomic mobility permits more complete atomic mixing than rapid heating and cooling.
More complete atomic mixing reduces phase separation, elemental segregation, and uncontrolled morphology.
The initial material comprises more than five elements in near-equal ratios.
Rapidly heated and cooled baseline nanoparticles tend to exhibit phase separation, elemental segregation, and irregular particle morphology.
The controlled intervention consists of slower heating to an intermediate temperature, an isothermal hold, and controlled cooling.
The relevant processing window is approximately 300–800 °C, with the exact window depending on the alloy system.
Au-Ag-Cu-Pt-Pd and similar noble-metal mixtures have sufficiently moderate atomic-radius and mixing-enthalpy differences for the proposed intervention.
Local atomic diffusion dynamics are modulated by diffusion activation barriers and surface-energy differences among the constituent noble metals.
Rapid thermal processing provides insufficient time for uniform atomic diffusion.
Insufficient diffusion time kinetically traps segregated or phase-separated regions.
Slower heating and an isothermal hold give atoms time to overcome diffusion barriers and attain a more homogeneous distribution.
More homogeneous atomic mixing stabilizes the desired single-phase solid solution and a uniform particle morphology.
Relative to the rapid-processing baseline, the modified protocol will produce a more uniform elemental distribution.
Relative to the rapid-processing baseline, the modified protocol will reduce phase separation and elemental segregation.
Relative to the rapid-processing baseline, the modified protocol will produce more controlled particle morphology.
The proposed mechanism applies principally to noble-metal systems containing at least five elements with moderate atomic-size and mixing-enthalpy differences.
Extreme atomic-size mismatch or very large mixing-enthalpy differences may prevent single-phase formation even under the modified thermal protocol.

Failure of the modified protocol to produce statistically significant improvements in elemental uniformity, phase purity, and morphology relative to the rapid-processing control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial-state scope requires more than five elements, but the named Au-Ag-Cu-Pt-Pd example contains exactly five, and the boundary further broadens applicability to at least five elements.
